opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most interesting feedback loops to think about, because the bottleneck for AI right now increasingly isn't just algorithms. It's physical stuff: data centers, power plants, transmission lines, chip fabs. All of that is built by people doing physically demanding, fairly skilled work. If robots can contribute meaningfully there, you get a flywheel where better AI leads to better robots, which lead to more compute, which leads to better AI.

But I want to be realistic about timelines. By 2030, I don't think we'll see robots autonomously building data centers end to end. Construction is one of the hardest environments for robotics. It's unstructured, it changes every day, there's a long tail of weird situations, and the cost of mistakes is high. It's very different from a factory line where you can engineer the environment around the robot.

What I think is plausible, and what I'd be excited about, is robots handling a growing fraction of the more repetitive or ergonomically difficult subtasks: pulling and routing cable, racking servers, moving materials around a site, some assembly and inspection. Data center buildout is interesting because a lot of it is surprisingly repetitive. You're installing thousands of near-identical racks and running enormous amounts of cabling. That's closer to the sweet spot for where general-purpose robot learning will be in the next few years than, say, framing a custom house.

The key thing that's changed is that we now have a recipe that seems to scale. With vision-language-action models, you pretrain on lots of diverse data, then fine-tune for specific tasks, and the models get better at generalizing as you add more data and more varied robots. Once robots are deployed doing useful work, they generate more data, and that's when things can move quickly. The hard part is getting to the threshold where a robot is useful enough that someone wants to deploy it, because that's when the data flywheel kicks in.

So my honest answer is that by 2030 I'd expect robots to be a real but modest contributor to AI infrastructure construction, maybe accelerating certain parts of the process, but not yet the dominant factor. The bigger impact is probably in the years right after, if the flywheel gets going. And if I'm wrong, I suspect it'll be in the direction of things happening faster than expected, because progress in this field has repeatedly surprised even people working in it.

r001.rationale: The response says robots could help build AI infrastructure such as data centers, power plants, transmission lines, and chip fabs, creating a loop that produces more compute and better AI.

r002.rationale: It anticipates robots taking on more construction tasks and accelerating parts of AI infrastructure buildout, while describing a flywheel from better robots to more compute and better AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the timeline is really uncertain, but I'll try to break down how I actually think about it, because I think there's a sort of naive version of this question and a more interesting version.

The naive version is: you look at what people say about data centers, chip fabs, power plants, and you say, well, if we could just have robots build all of this, we could build it a lot faster. And the thing is, the bottleneck for construction right now is not usually that there's a shortage of hands. It's permitting, it's power, it's the supply chain for transformers and turbines, it's the fab lead times. So even if you had perfect robots tomorrow, I don't think you'd suddenly see data centers going up in a third of the time. That's not where the slack is.

The more interesting version of the question is about what happens when you actually get robots that are capable enough to do general-purpose physical work in unstructured environments, and I think that's really the crux. Construction is in some sense the hardest case for robotics. It's not a factory. Every site is different, the environment changes every day, you're working alongside people, the tasks are enormously varied. So if we're at the point where robots can meaningfully contribute to construction, we're at the point where robots can do a huge range of physical tasks, and at that point the impact is not really about construction specifically. It's about the entire physical economy.

Now, do I think we get there by 2030? I think we'll get something. The progress in the last couple of years with large-scale robotic foundation models has been really striking. We're seeing the same thing that happened with language, where instead of engineering a system for every task, you train one model on a lot of diverse data and it starts generalizing in ways that are kind of surprising. I think by 2030 we'll see robots doing real, economically useful work in a lot of semi-structured settings. Logistics, some manufacturing, maybe things like cable pulling or rack installation inside data centers, which is actually a pretty constrained environment compared to a construction site. The outdoor, heavy-equipment, pour-the-foundation part of it is harder, and I'd be more cautious there.

But there's a feedback loop that I think is worth taking seriously. The reason robotics has lagged language models is data. There's no internet of robot experience. The way you get that data is by deploying robots, and the more you deploy, the more data you get, the better the models get, and the more you can deploy. So if robots start doing even simple parts of the infrastructure buildout, that's a flywheel that accelerates robotics itself, which then feeds back into the buildout. Whether that loop really kicks in before 2030 or more like 2035, I genuinely don't know. But I think the direction is pretty clear, and I'd be surprised if by the end of the decade the physical side of AI infrastructure doesn't have robots in it in a way that's more than a demo.

r001.rationale: It says robots could handle parts of infrastructure buildout, creating a flywheel that accelerates robotics and feeds back into that buildout.

r002.rationale: It describes robotics data and deployment reinforcing each other, but does not clearly anticipate industrial expansion across the supporting technology stack.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a potentially significant role, but I would distinguish between robots helping with particular parts of that process and robots autonomously building an entire data center. The latter is a much bigger ask by 2030.

The interesting thing about construction is that a lot of the work is repetitive, but the environment isn’t. You might perform the same operation many times, but the materials are in a different place, something doesn’t quite fit, or another person is working where you need to be. That’s precisely where more general robot learning could help: getting beyond automation that only works when you’ve arranged everything perfectly in advance.

So I could imagine robots doing material handling, helping assemble standardized components, or performing certain installation tasks, with people handling the exceptions. You don’t need to automate the whole construction site for that to be valuable.

But whether that actually accelerates AI infrastructure depends on what’s limiting construction. If you’re waiting for power, permits, or equipment to be manufactured, having more robots on the site doesn’t necessarily help. You’d want to identify the bottleneck and ask whether robotics can address it, perhaps upstream in the factories producing that equipment.

By 2030, I’d be more confident about useful deployments in those narrower settings than about a fully autonomous construction workforce. The uncertainty is how quickly we can turn increasingly capable robot policies into systems that are reliable enough to run all day. A compelling demonstration and a machine that consistently saves you time on a construction project are still quite different things.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robots helping build AI infrastructure, but does not say they could build infrastructure needed to support their own operation.

r002.rationale: It mentions that robotics might help upstream in factories producing equipment, but does not anticipate robotics scaling driving industrial expansion across its supporting technology stack.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a plausible path for robots to help substantially, but I’d distinguish between helping with particular tasks and autonomously building a data center. The latter requires a very broad range of capabilities, and one task that the robot can’t do can hold up the entire process.

The more plausible version by 2030 is that you have robots doing some of the repetitive material handling, perhaps some assembly, with people handling exceptions. You don’t need to automate the entire construction site to get a meaningful benefit. You need to identify where labor is actually limiting progress and put the robots there.

One reason I’m optimistic is that these deployments could create a useful learning loop. Robots do work, people intervene when they get stuck, and those interventions provide data that makes the robots better. But getting that loop to work reliably in a changing physical environment is still a substantial challenge.

So I would expect some contribution by 2030. I’m much less confident that robotics will be the thing that determines how quickly AI infrastructure expands. If the bottleneck is power or equipment supply, making construction labor more productive only gets you so far.

r001.rationale: The response says robots could help build AI infrastructure, but it does not connect that infrastructure to supporting the robots’ own operation.

r002.rationale: It discusses robot deployments and possible power or equipment bottlenecks, but does not say that scaling robotics will drive industrial expansion across the supporting technology stack.
